profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting for a survey paper submission in ML research, focused on the near-final section that compares generalist medical image segmentation models against task-specific approaches. The team has a complete draft, an evidence extraction sheet from the literature, a small internal anchor-analysis notebook, and a reproducibility appendix template. The agenda is to review whether the current comparison design, supporting artifacts, and trustworthiness discussion are strong enough for internal sign-off before the draft is sent to senior co-authors. The expected outcome is agreement on final revisions, what still needs to be stabilized, and whether the manuscript package is ready for co-author circulation this week.

members.name: Dr. Elena Rossi
members.role: Lead Survey Author and Principal Investigator
members.expertise: Medical image analysis, evidence synthesis, clinical ML translation
members.background: Elena leads an academic lab on trustworthy AI for radiology and has coordinated several multi-institution review papers; she owns the survey framing, cross-paper synthesis, and timeline for circulating the draft to senior co-authors.
members.private_state: She wants the paper to clear internal review today so the broader author team can comment before conference deadlines stack up; she is trying to avoid reopening the paper's structure or turning the survey into a benchmark study.
hidden_assumptions: The 'performance summary' means the manuscript-facing synthesis matrix that consolidates best-reported numbers from published papers after light harmonization by modality, supervision regime, and task family.
A 'fair comparison' in a survey is primarily about disciplined caveating, grouping non-comparable settings, and avoiding overstated causal claims rather than recreating a common training pipeline.

If the draft is 'ready for co-authors,' the key threshold is that the main text, headline figures, and evidence claims are stable; extraction logs and appendix checklists can still be cleaned up afterward.
The 'reproducibility pack' for a survey mainly means provenance of paper selection, extraction notes, and table lineage, not a fully frozen experimental artifact set.
The 'trustworthiness section' should foreground regulation, privacy, security, budget, and clinical translation because those are the survey's most distinctive contributions beyond raw performance.

members.name: Dr. Marcus Lee
members.role: Senior Research Scientist and Methods Reviewer
members.expertise: Segmentation evaluation, benchmark methodology, reproducibility auditing
members.background: Marcus previously worked on standardized evaluation protocols for medical imaging challenges and often serves as the internal reviewer who checks whether collaborative papers make claims that are methodologically supportable.
members.private_state: He wants to prevent the survey from sounding more experimentally grounded than it is and is using this review to make sure any co-author-ready draft already has defensible evidentiary scaffolding.
hidden_assumptions: The 'performance summary' refers to the internal results matrix that aligns a few representative generalist and task-specific models under one common post-processing and scoring pipeline so the narrative has an anchor point.

A 'fair comparison' requires at least one controlled substrate—shared split handling, preprocessing conventions, and metric scripts for anchor experiments—even if the rest of the paper is literature synthesis.
If something is 'ready for co-authors,' then the extraction logs, inclusion/exclusion notes, and reproducibility checklist are already stable enough that later edits will be mostly cosmetic.
The 'reproducibility pack' includes frozen notebook outputs, exact run settings for the anchor analyses, and traceable links from every summary claim back to a stable artifact bundle.

The 'trustworthiness section' should operationally connect to the evidence by discussing failure modes, annotation mismatch, domain shift, and robustness limits, not only policy and compliance themes.

misalignment_points.topic: What the performance summary refers to
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the performance summary' as the thing that needs a final cleanup.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the manuscript synthesis matrix summarizing literature-reported results across zero-shot, few-shot, adapter, fine-tuning, SAM 2, and multimodal model families.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the internal anchor-analysis results matrix from the lab notebook, where a small subset of representative models was rerun or normalized under a common scoring setup.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both artifacts already circulate in the project folder under similar names, both summarize results, and both genuinely do need cleanup, so the phrase feels perfectly natural and never triggers a referent check.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the paper needs a 'fair comparison' between generalist and task-specific methods.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a careful survey comparison that groups papers by setting, flags heterogeneity in datasets and budgets, and states caveats clearly enough that readers can interpret trends responsibly.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the paper should only use strong comparison language if it is grounded by at least one apples-to-apples anchor analysis with aligned preprocessing, split conventions, and evaluation scripts.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like shared methodological common sense, and both are trying to be rigorous; because neither is disputing fairness as a value, the narrower versus broader definition remains hidden.

misalignment_points.topic: What artifact must be stable before the draft is ready
misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss whether the manuscript package is 'ready for co-authors' once the extraction logs are cleaned up.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks 'ready for co-authors' means the extraction logs are complete enough to support the current tables and can still undergo formatting, deduplication, and note polishing after circulation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks 'ready for co-authors' means the extraction logs and reproducibility checklist are already frozen enough that every table row, exclusion decision, and anchor-analysis note is stable before circulation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both agree the logs should be cleaned up and both expect some polishing in any draft process, the disagreement is about the threshold of sufficiency for the same artifact rather than whether the artifact matters at all.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both endorse strengthening 'the trustworthiness section' before the paper goes out.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means expanding discussion of regulatory compliance, privacy, security, compute budget, and clinical translation constraints highlighted in the survey framing.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this also includes technical trustworthiness tied to the comparison evidence, such as annotation ambiguity, failure cases on rare anatomies, sensitivity to prompt quality, and domain-shift robustness.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In current ML writing, 'trustworthiness' naturally bundles governance and technical reliability, so both hear a broad umbrella term that seems fully shared even though they silently draw the boundary in different places.

turns.inner_thought: I need a clean internal go-ahead today so I can get this out to the senior co-authors before everyone's schedules collapse. I do not want this review to spiral into restructuring the paper or turning the survey into a benchmark exercise. For me, the threshold is that the narrative, core figures, and synthesis claims are stable; the extraction logs can still get tidied after circulation. And before it goes out, the trustworthiness section should better foreground regulation, privacy, security, compute burden, and translation constraints, since that's where the survey adds value beyond a list of numbers.
